claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure developed through controlled heat treatments.
SRO correlation length, atomic clustering, and interface density can serve as surrogate markers for barriers to dislocation nucleation and crack initiation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Atom probe tomography can quantitatively map SRO and detect changes induced by heat treatment.
The proposed atom-probe measurements can quantify correlation length, clustering, interface density, and defect distributions.
In-situ TEM can verify the relevant dislocation activity during deformation.
A physics-informed machine-learning model using SRO and defect metrics can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior.
The proposed model will improve predictive accuracy for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture resistance by approximately 10–15% relative to established full-field simulations.
The proposed model will reduce computation time by more than 50% relative to conventional full-scale simulations.
Controlled heat treatments can systematically vary the degree of SRO.
The framework is intended to operate from room temperature to 673 K under quasi-static and high-strain-rate tensile and fracture conditions.
Local SRO and hierarchical defect distributions mediate the relationship between atomic-scale ordering and macroscopic elastic and fracture responses.
Spatial variations in SRO directly alter local resistance to dislocation emission.
Spatial variations in SRO directly alter local resistance to crack initiation.
SRO modulates the energy barriers governing plastic deformation and fracture.
SRO-based machine learning can map atomistic data to macroscopic mechanical behavior without complete full-field simulations.
Zones with distinct SRO will correlate with the observed onset of dislocation nucleation and crack initiation.
Traditional full-field microstructure simulations are computationally intensive and slower for predicting mechanical behavior.
Microstructural factors other than SRO may dominate the mechanical response.
Preliminary evidence supports a link between SRO and dislocation dynamics.

The hypothesis is predeclared to fail if independent measurements show no statistically significant SRO-event correlation or if the model does not achieve the anticipated accuracy improvement across multiple tests.
